eastern-dedicated-freight-corridor.confidence_note: Indian courts and tribunals record the project's land takings and several of the card's grievances from outside the lender, on the stretch the Comptroller and Auditor General says the Bank financed (Ludhiana-Khurja-Kanpur-Mughalsarai, 1,183 km, CAG Report No. 48 of 2015). The Central Administrative Tribunal at Allahabad recorded on 3 April 2012 that no decision had been taken on the job-in-lieu-of-land representation of 16 land losers of village Matkutta, Tehsil Sakaldeeh, Chandauli, filed on 3 September 2011. The Allahabad High Court recorded on 10 February 2025 that compensation on a Chandauli award of 1 June 2023 was still unreleased pending an enquiry into shares, and on 14 March 2024 quashed an order recovering part of the compensation already paid to two Chandauli landholders because the inquiries behind it were ex parte. On 12 December 2022 the same court recorded that land at village Kalna Gaharwar, Mirzapur had neither been acquired nor sold to the corridor while construction was at the verge of completion, and said entry on it without due process would be unlawful. What no outside document carries is the card's central claims: the 85,000 project-affected people, the count of families paid at pre-2013 rates, and the unrest and protest claims. What the Mirzapur order does not record is harm done: the demolition without payment is the petitioners' pleading, the court's finding is only that the land had not been acquired or sold, and the court told the owners to go and settle a price so the project would not halt. One case was dismissed with costs for concealment (Ram Kishun, 18 March 2021), which cuts the other way. The card stays contested because its quantities are the lender's alone, because no judgment records the corridor's harm as done rather than threatened, and because the two judgments with findings of official wrongdoing sit outside the stretch the Comptroller and Auditor General says the Bank financed.

field_changes.community: Across the three loans, nearly 85,000 people in about 1,000 villages in four states were affected by land acquisition (4,336 hectares). The World Bank reports many complaints from people paid lower rates used before India's 2013 land law raised compensation, and unrest over unpaid or late compensation that disrupted construction in some places. Some families went to court seeking the better terms given to 265 neighbouring households. In Chandauli, farmers in Cheeto village held a sit-in from 25 February 2016, and CPI (ML) Liberation workers began a hunger strike on 11 July 2016. They said promised jobs, market-price compensation and rehabilitation were not given. Indian court and tribunal records from the same districts show what the disputes looked like. Sixteen land losers of village Matkutta, Tehsil Sakaldeeh, Chandauli asked the Central Administrative Tribunal at Allahabad for the job the Railway Board's policy of 16 July 2010 promised people who lost land; the tribunal recorded on 3 April 2012 that their representation of 3 September 2011 had not been decided, and gave the Railways two months to decide it. In village Akbarpur, Tehsil Sakaldiha, Chandauli, the award of 11 March 2013 priced seven houses standing on one plot, gata 99, at between 40,800 and 832,200 rupees (Allahabad High Court, 18 March 2021, a petition the court dismissed with 20,000 rupees in costs for concealing that the family had been paid). At village Dharna in the same district the High Court recorded on 10 February 2025 that compensation under an award of 1 June 2023 had still not been released while an enquiry into shares went on. In Mirzapur the High Court recorded on 12 December 2022 that land at village Kalna Gaharwar had neither been acquired nor sold to the corridor, and said it would be unlawful for the Railways to enter it without due process; the owners said the authorities had begun demolition without paying. In Gautam Budh Nagar, where the corridor was built with government money after the Bank dropped the Khurja-Dadri stretch, the High Court held on 27 August 2021 that landholders of villages Chamrawali-Boraki, Rithauri and Hazratpur had filed objections which were never heard or decided, and that the competent authority told the Ministry of Railways on 24 September 2019 that no objections had been filed; it refused to quash the acquisition because the line was nearly finished, ordered compensation at current market rates, and required the respondents to hold an inquiry into who had submitted the incorrect report, sending a copy of the order to the Chief Secretary of Uttar Pradesh to see that the inquiry happened. In Bihar the Patna High Court set aside on 27 June 2014 the compensation orders the Commissioner-cum-Arbitrator had passed for more than thirty landholders of village Barej, Mohania, Kaimur without notice or hearing, and sent them back to be heard.

corrections: The card calls the project 'Uttar Pradesh, India' and places the harm in that state; the Comptroller and Auditor General's Report No. 48 of 2015 (chapter 3) states that the World Bank agreed in May 2011 to fund only the Ludhiana-Khurja-Kanpur-Mughalsarai stretch of 1,183 km, and the court records of corridor land disputes sit in Gautam Budh Nagar, Chandauli and Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh and in Kaimur in Bihar. The Kaimur cases are on the Mughalsarai-Sonnagar section, which that CAG chapter lists separately from the Bank-funded stretch, so they are corridor harm but probably not Bank-funded corridor harm; the Gautam Budh Nagar cases are on the Dadri spur, which the card itself says the Bank dropped. The Mirzapur cases are inside the Bank's stretch: the Railways told the Allahabad High Court in the Ajay Kumar case that the works at kilometre 155+030 in Mirzapur belong to the corridor's Mughalsarai-to-Prayagraj section, and Prayagraj lies between Kanpur and Mughalsarai.

The card's outcome field reports the lender's finding that no land acquisition issues were pending at closing. Allahabad High Court orders of 14 March 2024, 10 February 2025 and 8 April 2025 and a Patna High Court order of 27 June 2014 show compensation, apportionment and rehabilitation claims on corridor land still unresolved in court well after the loans closed, including an award of 1 June 2023 whose money had not been released by February 2025.

The writer's note that the CAG chapter contains no land finding is too wide. The chapter carries no land-acquisition or resettlement finding about affected people, but it does make a land finding of cost: it attributes an increase of 4,442 crore rupees in land cost to escalation, against the background of changes in the alignment.
eastern-dedicated-freight-corridor.what_the_outside_source_settles: That land and houses were taken for this corridor from named families in named villages of Chandauli and Mirzapur, with dates and awarded sums; that the Railway Board's job-in-lieu-of-land policy generated claims from Chandauli land losers that went undecided, which is the jobs grievance the card attributes to protesters and to a political party; that compensation on corridor land in Chandauli was still unreleased in 2025 and had been clawed back ex parte in one case; that in Gautam Budh Nagar the competent authority reported to the Ministry of Railways that no objections had been filed when objections had been filed, and a High Court ordered an inquiry into who did it; and that in Kaimur an arbitrator fixed compensation for more than thirty landholders without hearing them.
eastern-dedicated-freight-corridor.what_it_does_not_settle: None of the card's quantities. No outside document counts the 85,000 project-affected people, the 4,336 hectares, the families paid at pre-2013 rates, or the 265 neighbouring households said to have had better terms; nor does any outside document reach the Cheeto village sit-in of February 2016 or the July 2016 hunger strike, which remain a wire report of a party's claims. Nothing opened ties a death to the works. And the two judgments with the clearest findings of wrongdoing - Gautam Budh Nagar and Kaimur - are on stretches the CAG chapter and the card itself place outside the Bank's 1,183 km. Inside that stretch, the Mirzapur order of 12 December 2022 records a threatened wrong rather than a completed one: that the land had not been acquired or sold while construction was nearly finished, and that entry without due process would be unlawful. The demolition said to have begun without payment is the owners' pleading, not a finding.

Corrected what the court did about the false report: it required the respondents to hold an inquiry into the person responsible and sent a copy of the order to the Chief Secretary of Uttar Pradesh to ensure the inquiry happened. It did not ask the Chief Secretary to hold it.

Re-grounded the hold at contested. One of the writer's two stated reasons falls away, because Mirzapur is inside the Bank's stretch on a document rather than on geography. The hold now rests on the card's quantities being the lender's alone, on no judgment inside the Bank's stretch recording the harm as done rather than threatened, and on the Gautam Budh Nagar and Kaimur findings sitting outside the 1,183 km.

Added to the confidence note and to what_it_does_not_settle that the Mirzapur demolition is the petitioners' pleading, that the court's finding is only that the land had not been acquired or sold, and that the court directed the owners to settle a price so the project would not halt. what_i_verified_myself: CAG Report No. 48 of 2015, chapter 3, downloaded and read from disk with pdftotext. The sentence is there and the writer reports it accurately: the Ministry of Railways approached the World Bank in 2008 and, after field visits, meetings and appraisals, the Bank 'agreed (May 2011) to provide fund (US $ 2725 million equivalent to 13,625 crore) only for a stretch of Ludhiana-Khurja-Kanpur-Mughalsarai (1183 kms) section of Eastern Corridor', the first loan agreement signed October 2011 for US$975 million, the second unsigned as at March 2014. The chapter also lists Sonnagar-Mughalsarai and Durgwati-Karwandia as separate sections in its delay findings, which is what puts the Kaimur cases outside the Bank's stretch. Its only land content is cost.

One qualification on that boundary, which I record rather than write onto the card: the same chapter uses 'Ludhiana-Khurja Dadri Section' as the name of a single civil and systems contract section, so the chapter by itself does not cleanly place the Khurja-Dadri spur inside or outside the 1,183 km. The exclusion of Khurja-Dadri rests on the Bank's own documents, which the card already cites, not on the CAG.

The Mirzapur section question, which the writer named as a weak call, resolves with a document. In Ajay Kumar and Another v. Union of India, Allahabad High Court, 11 August 2022, opened at indiankanoon.org/doc/192209685/, counsel for the Railways states that 'the total estimated cost of DFCC project from Pt. Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Junction to Prayagraj Junction is more than Rs.3,000 crores' and that the petitioners' house at kilometre 155+030 in village Pirallipur, Tehsil Chunar, District Mirzapur obstructs a 181 kilometre section otherwise almost complete. Prayagraj sits between Kanpur and Mughalsarai, so Mirzapur falls inside Ludhiana-Khurja-Kanpur-Mughalsarai. The rest of the writer's entry on this case checks out: resumption of Gaon Sabha land by the Commissioner, Vindhyachal Division, compensation of 33,42,507 rupees determined and uncollected, petition dismissed and the interim order of 3.1.2019 discharged.

Which contract section the Chandauli villages of Matkutta, Akbarpur and Dharna sit on. They are inside Chandauli, the district Mughalsarai is in, so they are at the eastern end of the Bank's stretch, but no document I opened states a chainage for them.

nagapattinam-canal-demolition-tsunami-re.confidence_note: The demolition without compensation is stated plainly in the Bank's completion report, which was opened for this round and says at paragraph 53 that the local authorities demolished the affected structures without offering compensation and assistance, and names the North Buckingham canal and Nagapattinam district. It is repeated in the Independent Evaluation Group's review. Both are the lender's own documents and neither names the stretch of canal or the village. Indian Kanoon holds no judgment that pairs a Buckingham canal with Nagapattinam, and nothing on this demolition was found in the index or on the web; no Indian court record, state audit or press report of it was found. One unrelated harm on the same project in the same district is on the court record: 74 beneficiaries of village Periyakuthagai, Vedaranyam taluk, Nagapattinam asked the Madras High Court in 2012 to order the completion of the reinforced-concrete-roof houses of package 22 under the project and 500 rupees a month until handover, and the petition sat for ten years and was dismissed for non-prosecution on 13 October 2022. That is a different set of people and different works, so it does not move the card. The completion report also does not say whether the sixth family was ever paid.

lucknow-muzaffarpur-highway-land.confidence_note: Allahabad High Court records carry the harm and name the works. The widening of National Highway 28 from kilometre 9 to kilometre 360.57, Lucknow to the Uttar Pradesh-Bihar border, was notified under section 3A of the National Highways Act 1956 on 26 May 2004; the parcels at Malinpur in Barabanki were notified separately, gazetted 1 June 2005. In the case of Ram Awadh of village Malinpur, Tehsil Ramsanehighat, Barabanki, the award of 31 August 2006 priced his land at 4.20 rupees a square foot; the District Magistrate of Barabanki, sitting as arbitrator, raised it on 18 September 2015 to 52 rupees a square foot with 9 per cent interest from the date of possession, and on 16 April 2019 the High Court recorded that the National Highways Authority had not deposited the enhanced sum and dismissed his petition for it, because the Authority's challenge to the award was still pending. For Barabanki landholders whose award was made on 7 December 2005 at agricultural rates, an arbitral award of 20 May 2015 found the land should have been valued as non-agricultural, at 490 rupees a square metre after a 30 per cent deduction; the Authority's objection was dismissed by the Additional District Judge, and on 31 October 2023 its twenty-one appeals were held time-barred on limitation alone, without the valuation being examined. At Basti, Savitri Devi's plot 294 (renumbered 323) of 0.038 hectare with the house on it was acquired for the same highway; on 5 July 2024 the High Court set aside the part of the arbitral award of 11 December 2008 that dealt with the land and sent it back to be recalculated. What the judgments do not do is name the World Bank loan and these parcels together. None of them mentions the Bank, and Indian Kanoon holds no judgment pairing the Bank with this highway or with the project's name. The link between these parcels and the Bank's money is an inference through the works, and this is what it rests on: the completion report restructured the project to Lucknow and the Uttar Pradesh-Bihar border, 328 kilometres of Bank-financed stretches inside a 358-kilometre corridor, delivered in eight contract packages, with the four packages in Bihar removed and all eight remaining packages in Uttar Pradesh; the borrower's own section of that report names Barabanki and Basti among the cities the project passes through; the 30 kilometres of the corridor the Bank did not pay for is the Gorakhpur bypass, in Gorakhpur district; and the Allahabad High Court recorded on 16 October 2025 that Package 2 of the Lucknow-Muzaffarpur Road Project was the four-laning of NH-28 from kilometre 45 to kilometre 92 of the Lucknow-Ayodhya section under a contract of 5 October 2005 for 2,123,344,969 rupees, which matches that report's own annex for Package II at 47 kilometres and 212.34 crore rupees. Barabanki lies on that chainage. No document ties any individual parcel to the loan. The counts on the card - 442 hectares, 14,976 titleholders and 8,418 people without title - remain the lender's own and are not corroborated anywhere outside it.

field_changes.community: The Bank's completion report describes the project's displacement and resettlement impacts as 'high in magnitude as well as intensity' and counts the taking of 442 hectares of private land from about 14,976 titleholders and 8,418 people without title, and 259 religious properties. It says that by the closing date land acquisition and resettlement were fully completed and all affected families had received their compensation and main entitlements, except a few whose cases were in court over who owned the land. Court records of the same works tell a different story about what was in court. The land was taken under section 3A of the National Highways Act 1956. One notification of 26 May 2004 covered kilometre 9 to kilometre 360.57, Lucknow to the Uttar Pradesh-Bihar border. The parcels at village Malinpur, Tehsil Ramsanehighat, Barabanki were notified separately, by a notification gazetted on 1 June 2005 and declared on 18 October 2005. Ram Awadh of Malinpur was awarded 4.20 rupees a square foot on 31 August 2006; the District Magistrate of Barabanki, sitting as arbitrator under section 3G(5), raised that to 52 rupees a square foot with 9 per cent interest on 18 September 2015, and on 16 April 2019 the Allahabad High Court recorded that the National Highways Authority had still not deposited the enhanced amount and dismissed his petition for it, because the Authority's own challenge to the award was pending and the rules barred payment until it was decided. Barabanki landholders whose award was made on 7 December 2005 by the Special Land Acquisition Officer, who treated the land as agricultural, won an arbitral award on 20 May 2015 holding that land within 100 metres of the highway should have been paid for at non-agricultural rates, 490 rupees a square metre after a 30 per cent deduction, with 9 per cent interest from the date of acquisition. The Authority's objection was dismissed by the Additional District Judge at Barabanki, and on 31 October 2023 the High Court held the Authority's twenty-one appeals against that dismissal to be time-barred, eighteen years after the award; it decided them on limitation alone and did not examine whether the valuation had been too low. At Basti, Savitri Devi's plot of 0.038 hectare and the house on it were acquired for the same highway, and on 5 July 2024 the High Court set aside the land part of the arbitral award of 11 December 2008 as patently illegal and sent it back to the arbitrator to be recalculated. Four religious properties could not be moved because religious leaders took hard positions. Stretches of land totalling up to 1,800 metres were taken out of the project because ownership disputes took too long to settle; the highways authority said it would do that work with its own money. Over the life of the project the Bank's own ratings for resettlement implementation moved from satisfactory to unsatisfactory and back to satisfactory. The consultants who were to evaluate what happened to resettled people at the end of the project were not hired until the closing date, so that evaluation was still under way; the Independent Evaluation Group says the Bank would keep monitoring it until the final report was submitted. The Independent Evaluation Group notes that the completion report does not state that all safeguards were met or complied with. At stakeholder workshops the general view reported was that land acquisition and resettlement 'was done reasonably well except for a few stray cases of dissatisfaction', and that landowners along the road were pleased because their asset values had risen; many people at the same workshops said road safety had worsened because of higher speeds.

corrections: The card repeats the completion report's statement that by the closing date all affected families had received their compensation and main entitlements, except a few whose cases were in court over who owned the land. The cases on the Allahabad High Court's record are not about who owned the land. They are about how much the land was worth: landowners at Barabanki and Basti were paid at agricultural or disputed rates, arbitrators appointed under section 3G(5) of the National Highways Act found the rates too low, and the National Highways Authority of India then litigated against paying the enhanced amounts until 2019, 2023 and 2024 - seven to twelve years after the loan closed on 30 June 2012.

The card's confidence note says no press report, court record or NGO field research on this corridor's resettlement was found. Three Allahabad High Court judgments on the corridor's compensation exist and are cited above; the note should be replaced.
lucknow-muzaffarpur-highway-land.what_the_outside_source_settles: That the takings on this card happened, under which law and on what dates, in which districts, and that compensation on at least part of the corridor was first fixed at agricultural rates and then found by the state's own arbitrators to be too low. It also settles that payment of the corrected amounts was not complete when the loan closed and was still being fought in 2023 and 2024, with named parties, named villages and plot numbers, and case numbers.
lucknow-muzaffarpur-highway-land.what_it_does_not_settle: The scale. The judgments cover one landowner at Malinpur, twenty-one sets of respondents at Barabanki and one at Basti; nothing outside the lender counts the 442 hectares, the 14,976 titleholders or the 8,418 people without title, and nothing supports the ICIJ figure of 75,434. Nor do they say anything about the 259 religious properties, about anybody losing a home as against part of a field, or about what happened to people without title, who cannot bring an arbitration over the value of land they do not own. No outside source was found for the end-of-project assessment of resettled people that the Bank never completed. They also do not name the World Bank. Nothing opened ties the loan to any particular parcel; that link runs through the corridor, the statute, the implementing authority and the contract-package chainage, and the card now says so.

dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.confidence_note: The Dehlon sequence, the two fatal accidents and the blocked entrances all come from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of the Bank's completion report, which cites that report paragraph by paragraph; the completion report itself is not disclosed. Indian Kanoon holds no judgment on the Dehlon plot. The High Court case the review describes - filed in May 2017 by a co-owner who refused the compensation offered, heard on 31 January 2018 without the plaintiff appearing - was searched for by the bypass name, by the project name and by the implementing board's name and does not appear in the index; Punjab and Haryana High Court orders of this kind are often not reported there. What the index does hold are two Income Tax Appellate Tribunal orders on the concessionaire that operates the road, which record that the Punjab Roads and Bridges Development Board developed the 71.352 km Ludhiana-Malerkotla-Sangrur road under World Bank aid and that the Dehlon bypass runs 'km 18+750 to km 20+800 of 2.98 km length', two statements of its size that do not agree, since that chainage spans 2.05 km; they say nothing about any plot, owner or payment. A High Court judgment of 6 June 2016 on the project's tendering confirms the Bank loan from outside the lender but concerns which contractor was eligible to bid. The Board's own website lists the bypass's acquisition papers under the 2013 land law, including a second unclaimed-compensation notice and an announcement of award; the notice, read through a fetch tool, is undated and names no project, so it cannot be tied to this plot or these dates. Nobody is named except by role, the drains that blocked 'numerous' entrances are not counted, and the two deaths are recorded in one sentence with no detail at all.
